kurz: Why price strength in the capital market persists for months, and why momentum strategies can give back their gains within a few weeks.

bloecke.md:
Two shares come from the same industry and have the same valuation ratios. One trades 40% above its price of twelve months ago, the other 30% below it. Under a strict reading of market efficiency, this should make no difference to future returns, because the past price history is public knowledge and has long been reflected in prices. A hundred years of data say otherwise.

Momentum refers to the finding that the relative price strength of the past six to twelve months predicts relative performance over the next three to twelve months. This finding is difficult to reconcile with efficient markets. It can hardly be interpreted as a risk premium and directly contradicts the weak form of the efficient market hypothesis. Nevertheless, it is the most widely replicated finding in empirical financial market research.

## Two often confused types of momentum

In [[Cross-sectional momentum|cross-sectional momentum]], all securities in a universe are ranked by their past return. The strategy buys the top decile and sells the bottom decile short. The direction of the market plays no role here: the bet is on relative strength alone. Jegadeesh and Titman documented this factor in 1993, and in 1997 Carhart included it in his model as a fourth factor alongside market, size and value.

[[Time-series momentum]], known in practice as trend following or absolute momentum, compares each instrument only with itself. If its own twelve-month return was positive, a long position is taken; if it was negative, the strategy switches to cash or goes short. In 2012, Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen found this effect in all 58 futures markets they examined, spread across equity indices, bonds, commodities and currencies. In 2013, Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen showed that value and momentum occur together in eight markets and asset classes.

In a bear market, the two variants behave differently. Cross-sectional momentum stays fully invested, because some security is always relatively stronger than the others, while time-series momentum exits the market. One strategy is a relative bet, the other a bet on the direction of the market.

bloecke.unter: Long-short factor portfolio (Winners minus Losers) and market risk premium, indexed to June 1963 = 1, logarithmic axis, last value July 2026.

bloecke.md:
## Empirical evidence

Over the full period from January 1927 to July 2026, the US momentum factor earns 6.07% a year geometrically and 7.41% arithmetically, with a volatility of 16.3%. After the market, this is the highest raw premium of the standard factors. Value stands at 3.59%, size at 1.42% and the market risk premium at 6.85%. Measured from July 1963, momentum at 6.33% a year is just ahead of the market at 6.15%.

The robustness of the premium matters more than its size. In 2016, Harvey, Liu and Zhu pointed out that the usual significance threshold of t = 1.96 no longer means anything when hundreds of factors are tested, and called for a hurdle of t > 3.0. Hou, Xue and Zhang then replicated 447 published anomalies, 85% of which failed the hurdle of t > 3.0. Momentum reaches t = 4.55 over a hundred years and thus belongs to the small group of factors that hold up even after strict correction for multiple testing.

The last column is the most informative for investors. Momentum was negative in one in five rolling ten-year windows since 1927, and still in 9.3% of cases for twenty-year windows. For private investors, there is no investment horizon that guarantees this premium.

bloecke.titel: Momentum and value by decade, USA
bloecke.unter: Geometric annual return of the long-short factors. The two series clearly take turns, and this is the most important reason for holding both factors together.

bloecke.md:
The decade marked with an asterisk covers only January 2020 to July 2026.

## Momentum crashes

The high premium comes with a return distribution that has a very long left tail, that is, with rare but very large losses. The factor lost 52.8% in 2009 as a whole, 34.4% in April alone and a cumulative 49.4% from March to May. The losses in 1932 were even higher, at −45.6% in July, −52.6% in August and −64.5% for the full year. The maximum drawdown ran from June 1932 to September 1939 and amounted to 78.4%. The old level was not regained until December 1956, after just under 24.5 years.

bloecke.unter: The market reached its low on 9 March 2009. Immediately afterwards, prices on the short side of the momentum portfolio rose sharply.

bloecke.md:
The crashes always follow the same pattern. After a deep slump, the loser side consists of highly indebted companies whose shares have fallen sharply and whose market beta has risen well above one. A portfolio that has sold these securities short holds a position with a strongly negative market beta during the recovery, just when the market is rising fastest. Daniel and Moskowitz showed that these crashes are partly predictable. They occur after bear markets when volatility is high. A variant scaled dynamically according to volatility roughly doubles alpha and the Sharpe ratio.

On a year-end basis, the cumulative factor has still not regained its old high. At the end of 2008 it stood at 66.9, in July 2026 at 48.0. After eighteen years, it is thus still around 28% below its old high.

Describing momentum as “following the winners” leaves out half of the picture. The premium is earned in many unremarkable months and lost again in a few months of very heavy losses. A strategy with a historical maximum loss of 78% and 24 years to recovery is no substitute for a market portfolio. It is suitable only as a supplementary holding and, with leverage, carries a clear risk of ruin. For the same reason, the effect has not been eliminated by arbitrage. The associated risk materialises rarely, but then with heavy losses.

## Implementation and costs

Monthly re-formation leads to high turnover, and the costs of turnover erode the return of every anomaly. Chen and Velikov analysed 204 long-short anomalies, taking into account bid-ask spreads, the publication effect and modern trading technology. On average they arrive at 4 basis points a month, or around 0.5% a year. After correction for data mining, the best anomalies achieve at most 10 basis points a month.

Three further deductions lie between the academic factor and a product you can buy. First, every ETF is long only. The short side is dropped, market beta dominates, and only a fraction of the pure factor exposure remains. Second, every index provider defines momentum differently and adds capacity and capping rules. Third, the backtest used to advertise a product is systematically embellished. For smart beta indices, Huang, Song and Xiang measure around 3% excess return before the launch of the associated ETF and −0.5 to −1% afterwards. For 97 predictors, McLean and Pontiff find on average 58% lower returns after publication. Momentum itself is not exempt from this.

## Tax consequences of turnover in Germany

With shares held directly in a securities account, every sale triggers flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer). It amounts to 25% under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act), or 26.375% in total including the 5.5% solidarity surcharge, plus church tax where applicable. Section 20(9) EStG provides a saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000. However, the same provision rules out the deduction of income-related expenses (Werbungskosten), such as custody fees. Order costs for buying and selling, by contrast, reduce the capital gain (Section 20(4) sentence 1 EStG). Sales also follow FIFO (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG), that is, the order in which the purchases were made. For a position that is built up in tranches and partly sold, the oldest and usually largest gains are therefore inevitably realised first.

In a fund, things are different. Reallocations within an ETF are not a disposal for the investor. What is taxed are the distributions, the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) under Section 18 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) and the sale of the units. For equity funds, the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20(1) sentence 1 InvStG reduces the tax base. As a result, the effective burden falls from 26.375% to around 18.5%.

The assumptions are €10,000 invested, a gross return of 8% a year, 15 years and 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax. For simplicity, the saver's allowance is ignored.

- Without realisation, the investment grows to €10,000 × 1.08^15 = €31,722. Tax of €5,729 is due on the gain of €21,722, leaving €25,993 net.
- With full turnover every year, the net return falls to 8% × (1 − 0.26375) = 5.89% p.a. The final value is €10,000 × 1.0589^15 = €23,595.

The difference is around €2,400, that is, just over 9% of final wealth or about 0.7 percentage points of return a year. That is more than the expected net excess return of the average anomaly according to Chen/Velikov. A momentum strategy implemented with individual shares held directly in a securities account must first earn these 0.7 points on top of the spread and order fees.

## Value and momentum in combination

From July 1963 to July 2026, the monthly correlation between HML and the momentum factor is −0.19. This negative correlation follows from the way the two factors are constructed. Value strategies buy what has fallen for a long time, momentum strategies buy what has recently risen. In substance, both describe the same price dynamics from two sides. Momentum rests on underreaction to new information, value on the subsequent overreaction and its correction.

The decade chart above shows the consequences. In the 1990s, momentum delivered 13.7% a year while value stood at −0.35%. In the 2000s the relationship reversed, with 7.4% for value against −2.0% for momentum. Two return streams with negative correlation combine into a smoother path than either of them on its own.

However, the combination does not protect against simultaneous weak phases. In the 2010s, momentum was weak at 2.6% and value negative at −2.6%. Both factors can therefore disappoint at the same time, as that decade showed.

bloecke.md:
## Explanations for the momentum effect

There are four competing explanations, which are not mutually exclusive. The behavioural explanation rests on underreaction. Information spreads slowly, analysts adjust their estimates step by step, and the price follows the news with a delay. The second explanation points to the disposition effect. Investors sell winners too early and hold on to losers too long, which delays price adjustment and so creates the trend that momentum strategies exploit. The third is a risk-based explanation, according to which the premium is compensation for the strongly left-skewed distribution, that is, for crash risk. The fourth explanation is limits to arbitrage. Investors who have to account for their results every month do not deploy a strategy that can lose half its value in three months on an unlimited scale.

The state of research in 2026 is similar for all factors. The existence of the premiums for value, momentum, profitability and low risk is well documented. What is disputed is their future size after costs. A more realistic expectation is 0 to 2 percentage points a year over the market portfolio, combined with double-digit drawdowns and weak phases lasting ten to twenty years.

Momentum is one of the few classic anomaly findings that hold up after correction for multiple testing, over a hundred years and across asset classes and continents. At the same time, its premium is reduced most reliably by turnover, taxes and product dilution. An investment decision has to take both findings into account.

The academic factor is a long-short portfolio with no capital outlay. The proceeds from short selling the losers finance the purchase of the winners. However, securities lending is most expensive for precisely the sharply fallen securities that would matter, and margin calls coincide with the momentum crash.

A long-only ETF therefore holds only the upper half of the ranking. It mostly carries market beta, and the contribution of the short side is missing entirely. The 6.07% a year describes the upper limit of a construct that cannot be traded in this form, and it is not suitable as a return expectation for a product.

mitnehmen: Cross-sectional momentum bets on relative strength and stays invested in a bear market; time-series momentum bets on direction and then exits. When momentum is discussed, it should therefore always be stated which variant is meant.

After the market, momentum has the highest raw premium of the standard factors (6.07% p.a. since 1927, t = 4.55) and at the same time the most skewed distribution, with a 78% maximum drawdown and 24.5 years to recovery.
Momentum crashes occur at the turning point after deep slumps, because the losers that were sold short then rise the most. In April 2009, the factor's monthly return was −34.4%.

After turnover costs, around 0.5% p.a. remains of the average anomaly, and for direct holdings in a German securities account, annual realisation costs about 0.7 points more because the tax deferral is lost.
Value and momentum have a correlation of −0.19 and take turns over decades. The combination smooths the path but does not protect against joint weak phases such as in the 2010s.

begriffe.text: Strategy that ranks securities by their past return, buys the strongest and sells the weakest short. It bets on relative strength rather than on the direction of the market.

Also called absolute momentum or trend following. Each instrument is compared only with its own past. If the twelve-month return is positive, a long position is held; if it is negative, cash or a short position.

Abrupt loss of a momentum strategy at the turning point after a bear market, because the high-beta losers that were sold short rise the most in the recovery. One example is April 2009, with a monthly return of −34.4%.
Flat-rate deduction from the taxable income of investment funds under Section 20 InvStG. For equity funds it is 30%, which reduces the effective burden from 26.375% to around 18.5%.
